title: Proposed $70,000 OPT Fee Would Sharply Raise Cost of Student Work Permits
excerpt: A Department of Homeland Security proposal would charge schools $70,000 for a first OPT recommendation and $30,000 for each later one, including STEM extensions — up from about $500 today — with public comments open through November 9.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security has proposed a $70,000 fee for a student's first Optional Practical Training recommendation, up from a student-paid cost of about $500 today, plus $30,000 for each later recommendation including the STEM extension — up to $100,000 tied to one STEM graduate.
  • The fee would be paid by the student's school before a designated school official can enter the OPT recommendation in the federal tracking system; schools could pass the cost on to students or employers.
  • Reader check: this is a proposed rule, not in effect. Public comments run through November 9, and if finalised it would take effect 60 days after publication and would not apply to students already approved or recommended for OPT.
  • More than 294,250 students took part in OPT in 2024-25, roughly a quarter of all international students in the United States.

The Department of Homeland Security has proposed charging colleges $70,000 each time they recommend an international student for Optional Practical Training, the programme that lets F-1 students work in the United States in jobs tied to their studies after graduation. The proposal, published in the Federal Register on October 8, would replace a cost of about $500 that students currently pay and would add a $30,000 charge for each subsequent recommendation, including the 24-month extension for science, technology, engineering and mathematics graduates. For one STEM graduate who uses both, the fees tied to a single student could reach $100,000.

How the fee would work

OPT allows F-1 students to work for up to 12 months in a field directly related to their major, with STEM graduates eligible for a further 24 months. Under USCIS rules, any off-campus training employment must be related to the student's area of study and authorised in advance by the designated school official and USCIS. Under the proposal, the school would have to pay the fee before that official could enter a recommendation in the federal student tracking system, and the government would not grant work authorisation otherwise. The money would go to the Treasury. Schools could pass the fees on to students, to all students, or to employers, Insight Into Academia reported.

DHS says the fees are meant to curb fraud and protect American workers. The department says ICE has identified more than 10,000 potentially fraudulent cases tied to the programme. A DHS spokesperson said OPT was never meant to be "a back door into the American workforce," and the department argues the charge would push schools to scrutinise students more closely.

The numbers behind the proposal

More than 294,250 students took part in OPT in 2024-25, roughly a quarter of all international students, according to the Institute of International Education. DHS's own analysis projects the fees would bring in between $8.4 billion and $16.5 billion a year, with a primary estimate of $12.4 billion, and estimates annualised costs of about $4.1 billion, driven largely by lost OPT participation. DHS estimates 56 percent of the roughly 2,500 schools affected are small; by its count 841 would see costs exceeding 1 percent of revenue in the first year, with 116 above 20 percent.

"It's a really important bridge for international student graduates who want to stay and work in the United States."

— Julia Gelatt, Associate Director of the U.S. Program, Migration Policy Institute

Pushback from universities and employers

More than half of international students stay and work after graduating through OPT, Marketplace reported, and educators say the fee would break that bridge. "I imagine there would only be very few institutions who could even remotely entertain the notion of being able to cover that cost," said Clay Harmon, executive director of AIRC: The Association of International Enrollment Management. Fanta Aw, CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators, said the government has not offered enough evidence of widespread fraud to justify the cost and warned that "international students will find other destinations."

For Indian students — one of the largest international cohorts in the US and heavily represented in STEM programmes — the arithmetic is direct. OPT is the usual route from an F-1 visa into a first US job and, for many, later H-1B sponsorship. A $70,000 charge at the recommendation stage, whoever ultimately pays it, reprices that route before a graduate has earned a first salary.

What happens next

The proposal is open for public comment through November 9. UC Berkeley's International Office plans to oppose the rule, and NAFSA plans to file comments urging universities to do the same. If a final rule is issued, it would take effect 60 days after publication and would not apply to students already approved or recommended for OPT.
